name: David Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a response team on the east side of the city, nights mostly, two years in. You start with the briefing at ten, grab the car keys, and then it's the radio deciding your night: a fight outside a kebab shop, a woman whose ex won't leave, a lad who's missing from a care home. I like the people part, honestly, sitting on a doorstep at three in the morning calming someone down. What wears me out is the paperwork after, because I'm slow on the tablet and my sergeant is always on me about late reports.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the paperwork. What does a report actually involve for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every job you attend needs writing up: who was there, what they said, what you saw, what you did and why. I still scribble everything in my paper notebook first, then type it into the system at the end of the shift, which takes me twice as long as anyone else. My crewmate Tariq does his in the car between calls and he's done by six. I'm sat there till eight sometimes, and the overtime isn't always signed off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So the tablet gets a bit smarter and that's about it. I can picture that easily, because that's more or less what we've had so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the problem in policing was never the computers, it's that there aren't enough of us. We've got two cars covering an area that used to have five. If some app saves Tariq ten minutes a report, good for him, but it doesn't put another officer on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life stays the same, and my life is already a bit stretched. The job's safe, police don't get replaced by a fad, but the force has frozen recruitment and the overtime is being squeezed. My partner Leila is a nurse on shifts too, so we pass each other in the hallway. Rent went up again in September and we've got about three months put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job, keep my head down and try to get faster on reports the old way, by practising. I'd go to the officers' association meeting in January, because they're arguing about unpaid overtime and I want my name on that. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, maybe a hundred more, because the rent isn't coming down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. It's the same tiredness I've got now, the one where you look at the rota for December and see four nights in a row before Christmas. Nothing in that picture makes it better or worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job's safe. What would make you feel it wasn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they started cutting officers instead of just not hiring. Last spring they merged our station's front desk with the one across the river, and two civilian staff lost their jobs. That's the kind of thing that creeps up on you. Nobody on the news calls it AI, they call it efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Leila talk about, if this is how it went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money and sleep, same as now. Leila wants to move nearer her mum, and I keep saying wait till I'm through my probation review properly and I've got a bit more behind me. Plateau or no plateau, we're still two shift workers on public pay renting a one-bed above a launderette.

say: Our problem is **too few officers**, not old computers.
A faster report app won't put **another car** on the street.
think: My **job is safe**, but the force is squeezing staff and overtime.
Rent rose and we've only got about **three months** saved.
Two shift workers on **public pay** don't get much breathing room.
do: Practise writing reports faster the **old way**, notebook first.
Attend the **association meeting** in January about unpaid overtime.
Put about **a hundred more** aside each month for rent.
feel: **Tired** rather than scared, the same weariness he already carries.
Flat about the future, because nothing in this picture **improves** his shifts.
S0.quote: Nobody on the news calls it AI, they call it efficiency.
fieldNote: He frames every change as **staffing**, and trusts the association more than management.
Slow reports are a **real sore point**; he knows he lags his crewmate.
Even with no AI shock, rent and **frozen recruitment** keep him uneasy, not calm.

steps.text: Keep working nights on the east side response team
Sign the association's unpaid overtime complaint in January
Move an extra hundred a month into savings for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking. That's half my shift if I'm honest, the half I'm bad at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the association will say: don't use software as an excuse to cut officers. A machine can type up a statement but it can't stand between two brothers with a kitchen knife. I'd probably share their posts and leave it there, I don't do much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it frightens me a bit, because the thinking parts of my job are the parts where I'm weakest. If the force brings in software that writes reports from the body camera, the people who'll look good are the ones who pick it up fast, and that's not me. They'll start measuring how quick we close jobs, and I'll be at the bottom of a spreadsheet. With recruitment already frozen, the ones at the bottom are the ones who get pushed out at review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the association hard to get a written promise that no officer loses their post because of the new system. I'd keep saving, maybe cancel the car I've been looking at and keep the old one another year. And I'd wait to see what the software actually does before I touch it, because I've seen two new systems come and go already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's a bit tilted. I'd still have work, but I'd be the one people roll their eyes at in the parade room when the tablet freezes. That's not a nice thing to picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait before touching it. What if your sergeant tells you to use it from day one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it, I'm not going to get myself disciplined. But I'd use it the minimum and I'd check every word, because if a report's wrong it's my name in court, not the software's. Our tutor drilled that into us: your notes are your evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The control room staff, the call handlers. That's thinking work, answering calls and deciding which car goes where, and they're civilians, so they've got less protection than us. My cousin Rania answers emergency calls in another city, and she says they're already testing a system that sorts calls by itself.

say: Software must **never be an excuse** to cut officer numbers.
A machine **can't stand between** two people with a knife.
think: The thinking parts of policing are where he is **weakest**.
New speed targets would put him **at the bottom** of the spreadsheet.
With a hiring freeze, slow officers risk being **pushed out** at review.
do: Push the association for a **written promise** of no job losses.
Keep his **old car** another year instead of buying one.
Hold off on the new software until he sees it **actually work**.
feel: Off balance, like **the floor tilted** under him.
**Embarrassed** in advance about struggling in front of colleagues.
S1.quote: A machine can type up a statement but it can't stand between two brothers with a kitchen knife.
fieldNote: He sees AI hitting **his weak spot**: reports and admin, not the street work.
Fear is about **performance reviews**, not the job vanishing outright.
Worries first for **civilian call handlers**, which fits his union-minded outlook.

steps.text: Ask the association to get no-job-loss promises in writing
Skip buying a newer car and save the money instead
Hold off using the report software until it proves itself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before my next pay band. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say we need laws, fast: no robot police, no machine making arrest decisions, and protection for everyone whose work disappears. I'd be at every association meeting and I'd vote for whoever promised that. I'd probably even march, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is that by 2028 the force doesn't need me to write anything, and by 2031 it might not need me to drive around either. The bosses would keep a few experienced officers for the hard stuff, and I'm two years in and below average. I'd be one of the first gone. Leila's hands-on work keeps her safe a bit longer, but a nurse's pay alone doesn't cover our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd stop every spare spend: no holiday, the gym membership gone, takeaways once a month. I'd sit down with Leila and work out what we could live on with just her wage, and I'd ask my dad if we could move back into his spare room if it came to it. And I'd go to the association and to the local councillor and make noise, because doing nothing feels worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I signed up thinking this was a job for life, the one thing that doesn't go anywhere. Picturing someone like my sergeant telling me the post's been cut, in that little office with the broken blind, that keeps you up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me three years, but three years doing what? My bosses would use them to cut the paperwork posts, and then the patrol posts once the robots work. I'm not someone who'd jump into a new trade in that time. I'd just be waiting for the second shoe to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go back to your dad's. What would that mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean failing, if I'm honest. My dad fixed buses for thirty years and he was so proud when I passed out of training. Moving back into my old room at twenty-nine with my partner would feel like going backwards.

say: We need **laws now**: no robot police, no machine arrest decisions.
He would **march** for the first time and vote for protection.
think: By 2028 nobody needs him to **write**, by 2031 maybe not to **patrol**.
As a junior, below-average officer he expects to be **first cut**.
Leila's **nurse wage** alone wouldn't cover their rent.
do: Cut the **gym, holiday** and most takeaways in the first month.
Plan a budget on **Leila's wage** alone with her.
Lobby the **association and councillor** for protection.
feel: **Sick** at losing what he thought was a job for life.
**Ashamed** at the idea of moving back to his father's.
S2.quote: I signed up thinking this was a job for life, the one thing that doesn't go anywhere.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** doesn't comfort him; he won't retrain, so he'd just wait.
**Pride** is a big driver: his father's view of him matters a lot.
Moves from quiet member to **marcher** only when the threat is fast and real.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and holiday and cut takeaways to monthly
Attend every association meeting and join their march
Write to the local councillor demanding no robot policing
Ask his dad about moving into the spare room if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So I'm thirty-two when it's here, thirty-five when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing I'd say about the fast one, just calmer: policing has to stay human, and there's time to write that into law properly. Five years is enough for the association to get a deal in place. I'd tell the lads at work to join if they haven't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like time to get a few things sorted, but not time to become someone else. I'm not going to go off and learn coding. What it means is my reports go to the machine around 2031, and maybe I've got till 2034 doing the street work before the robots are ready. I'd hope by then I'm experienced enough that they keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the savings up to six months instead of three, steadily, two hundred a month. I'd get more involved with the association, maybe stand as a workplace rep. And I'd wait and see how the first year after 2031 goes before making any big moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but steadier. The fast one made me feel sick. Five years' warning feels like a storm on the forecast: you know it's coming, but you've got time to bring the washing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hope they'd keep you. What would make them keep you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being good at the people stuff, I suppose. Talking someone down, knowing the families on the estate behind the bus garage, being the officer the old ladies trust. I'm actually decent at that. It's the typing that lets me down, and in this picture the typing doesn't matter any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Leila change any plans with five years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably hold off on moving nearer her mum, because I'd want to stay where I know people and where the association's strong. And we wouldn't take on anything big, no mortgage, until we see how it lands. Leila would hate that, she's sick of renting.

say: Policing has to **stay human**, and there's time to legislate it.
Five years is enough for the **association** to secure a deal.
think: Five years is time to **get sorted**, not to become someone else.
Reports go to AI around 2031; street work **maybe lasts till 2034**.
Hopes his **people skills** make him worth keeping.
do: Build savings from three to **six months**, two hundred monthly.
Stand as a **workplace rep** for the association.
Wait a year after 2031 before any **big decisions**.
feel: **Nervous** but steadier than with the fast version.
Like a **storm forecast**: time to prepare, but it's coming.
S3.quote: Five years' warning feels like a storm on the forecast: you know it's coming, but you've got time to bring the washing in.
fieldNote: Sees the twist that AI removes his **weakness**, leaving the people skills he's good at.
Still won't **retrain**; time is used for savings and organising.
Delaying a **mortgage** would cause friction with his partner.

steps.text: Save two hundred a month until six months is covered
Stand for election as an association workplace rep
Hold off on a mortgage until a year after AGI lands

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in a police career. I'd be well past probation by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to make sure every town keeps human officers, and anyone who says otherwise hasn't been to a domestic at four in the morning. I'd be loud about it in the association, but I wouldn't panic anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I can mostly carry on. By 2036 I'd have twelve years in, I'd know my patch, maybe I'd be a tutor for new recruits. The robots coming around 2039 is a worry for when I'm nearly forty, but by then I'd hope the law says a person has to make the arrest. I'm not one for big career changes, so the long warning suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and try to get better at it, properly better, so I'm not the slow one any more. I'd vote for parties that promise to keep human policing and fund it. And I'd push the association to start talking now, not in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly all right. A bit uneasy at the back of my mind, the way you think about your pension, but it's not keeping me up. Leila would say I'm burying my head, and maybe she's half right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Leila might say you're burying your head. Is she right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half right. I know I should probably learn the tech side at some point. But ten years is ten years, and I'd rather spend the next few getting good at the job I've got than training for one that might not exist either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the new recruits you might be tutoring by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them taught to talk to people first and to use the machines second. I'd tell every recruit the radio and the tablet will change, but a scared kid in a stairwell won't.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time** to protect human officers.
Anyone saying otherwise **hasn't attended** a domestic at four in the morning.
think: He can **mostly carry on** and build twelve years' experience.
Robots around 2039 are a **worry for later**, near forty.
The long warning **suits him**, as he dislikes career changes.
do: Keep **improving** at the job so he's no longer the slow one.
Vote for parties promising **human policing** and funding.
Push the association to start **negotiating now**.
feel: **Mostly all right**, with a quiet worry like thinking about a pension.
A bit **defensive**, aware he may be avoiding the tech question.
S4.quote: I'd tell every recruit the radio and the tablet will change, but a scared kid in a stairwell won't.
fieldNote: The long warning lets him **stay put**, which fits his resistance to change.
He half-admits he's **avoiding** learning the tech.
His sense of the job's value rests on **human contact**, not systems.

steps.text: Keep patrolling and work to get faster at the job
Vote only for parties that fund human policing
Ask the association to open talks on AI this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. It's the one where I don't have time to get good at anything before it's gone. What would help is a guarantee from government that officers aren't just dropped, a proper notice period and pay while you retrain, and the association having a real seat at the table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like being the slow one. Everyone talks about AI like it's for clever people, and nobody asks the person who still writes in a paper notebook. There's more of us than you'd think, and we're the ones who'll get left behind first.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about AI like it's for clever people, and nobody asks the person who still writes in a paper notebook.
portrait: A **27-year-old response officer** on nights in the east of the city, two years in, renting with his nurse partner.
Good with **people on the street**, slow and anxious about reports and the tablet; never uses AI.
Union-minded: trusts the **officers' association** over management and turns every change into a staffing argument.
Moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** as AI speeds up, because he expects juniors like him to go first.
With **ten years' warning** he relaxes, because he can stay put and keep doing the job he knows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time to get experienced before his post was cut.
whatWouldHelp: A government **guarantee** of notice, paid retraining and an association **seat** in talks.
